opening.headline: We explore how session budgets and stage-by-stage cost tracking help mitigate the issue of costs accumulating silently during unmonitored overnight executions.
body: Suppose an agent started in the evening, repeatedly calling the same tool without stopping overnight, and by morning we find its accumulated cost had exceeded the expected limit. In executions unmonitored by a human, costs accumulate silently. Furthermore, an agent's cost increases not only in tokens but also in web search and execution time.

In this class, we examine how costs are measured at the step, call, and session levels, and how session-level budget settings are read at the per-unit level. We then verify how the agent pauses when budget limits are reached and how it resumes afterward, and use a case study to establish criteria for determining whether the budget limit is appropriate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the session budget and stage-based cost limits.
It is possible to determine whether the cost cap setting is appropriate.

screens.title: An agent running all night exceeded the budget.
screens.lead: First, let's examine the events that occurred during the night in chronological order. Read the following scene and consider at which point something happened.

visual.alt: A graph showing cumulative costs continuously increasing over time from evening to morning, exceeding the expected upper limit.

paragraphs: The agent that started in the evening repeatedly called the same tool without stopping throughout the night. When checked in the morning, the accumulated cost had exceeded the expected limit.

This happens because costs accumulate silently in executions that are not monitored by humans. While a single call may be small, repeated calls can result in unexpectedly high expenses by morning. Agent costs increase not only with model tokens but also with web search and session execution time. Therefore, focusing solely on tokens means overlooking important aspects.

What's needed is a mechanism that stops before costs exceed a threshold. The question to be answered in this course is this: what kind of mechanism can be put in place to halt before costs go beyond a limit?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: How to check costs in the morning is only informed after an incident occurs. Before an incident happens, at what point and how should costs be reviewed?

screens.outro: First, let's recall what limits may be placed on my agent execution.

screens.title: Is there a cost limit on agent execution?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Can the maximum cost per execution be expressed as a number?
items.answer: If the maximum cost cannot be expressed numerically, it is equivalent to having no upper bound. You should consider the worst-case scenario rather than normal expenditures. When an agent repeatedly re-enters the same stage due to an error, the key question is how far expenditures can go.

items.prompt: When the limit is reached, how is the agent configured to behave?
items.answer: Whether a process is fully terminated and cleaned up upon reaching a limit, or simply paused and resumed, determines the usefulness of that limit. If a process is paused and then resumed after root cause analysis confirms it can continue, setting a low limit imposes minimal burden. This lesson examines the different types of interruptions.

Simply having the habit of checking afterward will not reduce incidents. Events that notify usage during execution and invoices that confirm exact amounts afterward serve different purposes. We will also discuss methods for distinguishing between these two.

screens.outro: I've organized my thoughts now, so I'll first verify how costs are measured.

screens.title: How is cost measured: step, call, session
screens.lead: The following table summarizes the three units used for cost aggregation and the components of session costs. Read each row to verify the scope included by each unit.

data.caption: Cost measurement unit and components
rows: The usage of assistant messages sharing the same ID should be counted only once to avoid duplicate aggregation.
This is a single function call in an SDK that includes multiple steps.
After the call completes, the accumulated usage and estimated cost total_cost_usd are populated in the result message.
A bundle of multiple calls associated with a session ID
The result of the resumed call reports not only the cost of that call but also the overall session expenditure.
Model tokens, web search, and session execution time are continuously summed up as values in the public list.
Web search costs $10 per 1,000 queries, and session execution time is calculated at $0.08 per hour.
The exact amount can be verified on the Console's Usage page or via the Usage and Cost API.
The total_cost_usd of the SDK is a local estimate and is not billed to users or used as a basis for financial decisions.
data.notes: List costs are based on the published list price, not the contract price. If a discount applies, the actual billed amount may be lower than the limit. Cost tracking is currently under development and used for insights and rough budgeting purposes; accurate billing is always verified through billing documentation.

screens.outro: Now that we know the unit of measurement, let's examine the budget allocation setting when creating a session, on a per-unit basis.

screens.title: Read session budget configuration on a per-record basis
screens.lead: The following is code used to create a session and allocate budget within Managed Agents. By selecting the highlighted portion, you can view the meaning of that line and the symptoms that appear when it is incorrectly used.

marks.note: This is an optional hard limit when creating a session. A budget can only be attached when creating a session. Attempting to attach a budget to an already-running session will be rejected with error 400. Therefore, if a limit is required, it must be specified when creating a new session.
It's always a limit value. A fixed field with no reason to use any other value.

A string value representing an integer in U.S. cents, where 125 represents $1.25. It is a string rather than a number to prevent floating-point rounding issues. The value must be greater than zero, and values in decimal form such as "25.00" are rejected, causing session creation to fail.
This is an uppercase currency code. The supported currency is USD only.

This is a cap. This value is compared against the total session cost computed from the public list price. The limit is checked between model requests, so new model requests are not initiated upon reaching the limit, but ongoing requests are executed to completion.

screens.outro: Now that I've learned how to read the settings, I'll proceed to examine the events that occur when the limit is reached, in sequence.

screens.title: Flow where the agent stops when the budget cap is reached
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to verify the six steps from the moment the limit is reached until work is resumed.

visual.alt: Session flow where a running session reaches its limit, triggers an event, stops in idle state, and is restarted upon budget modification.
labels: Cumulative cost has reached the limit

steps.title: 1. The session is running.
steps.body: The session repeatedly makes model requests while in running state. The limit is checked between model requests, so before starting each request, verify whether the cost consumed so far exceeds the limit.

steps.title: 2. Accumulated cost reaches the limit
steps.body: The consumed list cost has reached the ceiling. From this moment on, all threads stop and do not begin the next model request. The last request that exceeded the limit started below the limit and thus completes execution fully.

steps.title: 3. The thread is halted.
steps.body: Each thread stops with the session.thread_status_idle event and stop_reason is budget_reached. Including the expenditure of requests that exceed the limit, the recorded cost may be equal to or slightly above the limit.

steps.title: 4. Usage events are coming.
steps.body: The session.usage event notifies about the accumulated usage and cost list_cost. This event always occurs immediately before the idle event. The app can read how much was consumed from this event.

steps.title: 5. The session remains idle.
steps.body: The session.status_idle event occurs together with stop_reason budget_reached. The session does not terminate; instead, it becomes idle, and records and sandboxes are preserved. In this state, any user.message initiating a new task is rejected with a 400 error, and only events that finalize ongoing operations—such as tool confirmation or tool results—are received.

steps.title: 6. If the budget is changed, it is reinitialized.
steps.body: Work that was paused will automatically resume when the budget is increased or removed via session update. No additional actions are required. The new limit must be greater than the costs already incurred.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the flow, let's illustrate why fatigue from overnight work is necessary using a real-world example.

screens.title: Explanation: Why overnight work needs a budget cap
screens.lead: Move the slider to compare how the same night-time error leads to different results depending on the upper limit height.

stops.body: A hypothetical data consolidation agent repeatedly loops through the same stage due to errors, running overnight. Without an upper bound, the accumulated cost curve continues to rise until morning. Since there is no protective mechanism in place until morning inspection, the potential damage is effectively infinite.

If the cap is lower than a typical normal operational expenditure, agents that were previously functioning properly will continue to stop. Since a human would have to manually increase the budget each time, the meaning of overnight automation is lost. The cost of operating at low levels becomes the repeated need to sustain operations. The belief that lower caps are safer is only half true. A balance must be struck between safety and continuity.

We set an upper limit by adding a buffer above the usual single-execution cost baseline. Even if an error occurs, the execution will stop at the upper limit and mark the state as budget_reached, after which no further costs will accumulate. The stopped session is considered idle; upon reviewing the logs in the morning to determine the cause, the budget can be increased and the session resumed. The new limit must be greater than the amount already consumed.

If the upper limit is too high, an incident may not be halted until much later. While an upper limit exists, if the maximum potential loss reaches several times the normal expenditure, the safety mechanism becomes weak. Since the limit is verified between model requests, the value must be set with consideration that it might be slightly exceeded.

screens.outro: Finally, let's walk through an example that examines the configuration and logs to identify the root cause.

screens.title: Explanation: Analyze settings and logs to identify the root cause
screens.lead: The instructor sequentially solves and explains four hypothetical cases. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next case.

steps.title: Example 1: Session creation is rejected for small amounts.
steps.body: "amount": "1.25" was specified, but session creation was rejected. The "amount" must be an integer string in cents, and decimal form is rejected for this reason. 1.25 dollars should be represented as "125".

steps.title: Example 2: Attempting to assign a budget to an ongoing session
steps.body: Attempting to add a budget to an existing session resulted in a 400 error. Budgets can only be assigned when creating a session, so they must be added when creating a new session. The budget limit of a session with an existing budget can be modified or removed at any time.

steps.title: Example 3: With a 50-cent limit, it stops at 53 cents.
steps.body: "amount": "50" but the list_cost is recorded as "53" and the process stops. This is not an error. Requests that exceed the limit begin below the limit and run completely within that boundary. Expenditures exceeding the limit occur only once per model request per thread, so the cap is set with a buffer for such cases.

steps.title: Example 4: Sending a message to a stopped session results in an error
steps.body: When sending a user.message to a session with stop_reason set to budget_reached, a 400 error occurs. This is because the event to start a new task is not received by sessions that have reached their limit. First, either increase the budget or remove the session, then restart and send the message.

steps.title: Determine the upper limit value
steps.body: If the ceiling is too low, normal operations will be halted and retries will be repeated; if it's too high, the risk of accidents increases. Set a reasonable ceiling above the typical baseline cost for a single execution, and distinguish between normal and abnormal executions based on tool call counts and token usage. Additionally, separate and review the estimated values reported by the SDK from the billing data in the Console.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: Cost is also a safety mechanism.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: Cost accumulates per step, call, and session, and includes tokens, web search, and execution time. Session budget stops new model requests when the limit is reached and puts the session in idle state. Changing the budget continues the operation.

The cost cap is a safety mechanism that sets a maximum level of potential damage in the event of an incident. When determining the cap value, consider both the usual expenditure baseline and the allowance to slightly exceed it.

glossary.def: This is an optional cap when creating a session. Requests for new models will be halted when costs reach the limit.
This is a cap mechanism that checks expenditures at step or call units and stops when the limit is reached.
This involves aggregating token usage and costs on a step, call, and session basis.
This is a rule that stops execution when the limit is reached and determines the state in which the session should be left.
The cumulative cost of a session, calculated as the sum of model tokens, web search operations, and session execution time, listed in an open inventory.

misconceptions.myth: The cost shown by the SDK is exactly the invoice amount.
misconceptions.fact: The SDK cost is an estimated value calculated locally. The exact billing can be verified on the Console's Usage page or through the Usage and Cost API.

misconceptions.myth: It terminates exactly at the limit amount.
misconceptions.fact: The limit is checked between model requests, so ongoing requests are executed to completion. The recorded cost may slightly exceed the limit.

misconceptions.myth: Sessions that have reached their limit are terminated and cannot be reused.
misconceptions.fact: The session remains idle and records and sandbox are preserved. Running tasks that were paused continue when budget is increased or removed.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: The cost accumulates on a step, call, and session basis and includes search and execution time.
The session budget stops new model requests when the limit is reached and leaves the session in an idle state.
The cost cap is a safety mechanism that limits the maximum potential damage during overnight execution.
The upper limit is set based on normal expenditure baseline, with allowance for slight exceedance of the limit.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: What is the maximum cost when my agent runs for the longest duration, and what mechanism ensures this value is not exceeded?

checks.q: When creating a session, a budget of {"type": "limit", "max_list_cost": {"amount": "2.50", "currency": "USD"}} was set to limit it to $2.50. What will happen then?
options: A session with a $2.5 limit is normally created.
Due to its fractional form being rejected, it must be written as the cent integer string "250".
Interpreted with a 2.5 cent limit, the session is immediately terminated.
The session is created, but the limit is ignored and only the cost is recorded.
checks.explain: amount must be a exact-string of US cents and decimal forms such as "25.00" are rejected. Two point five dollars must be represented as "250".

wrong.0: Decimal places in US dollars are not allowed.
wrong.2: A rejected form is not interpreted in any other unit.
wrong.3: If the format is incorrect, the request is rejected rather than the limit being ignored.
